item.title: This Year’s El Niño Is Huge and Already Changing the World
item.description:
El Niño is the planet’s naturally recurring chaos agent, scrambling weather patterns, spiking global temperatures and typically reaching full strength by December.

But this year’s El Niño, which is expected to be record-breaking, is already strong and having big effects, nudging up global temperatures and causing dry spells and crop failures on multiple continents.

Parts of Panama, normally one of the wettest countries on Earth, haven’t had a major storm since early May. Ethiopia’s fertile highlands are enduring one of their driest summer stretches in four decades. And India had its fifth-driest June since the country’s modern rain records began in 1901.

“This is a good sign that the El Niño response has really kicked in,” said Chris Funk, director of the Climate Hazards Center at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Dr. Funk termed it an “early onset El Niño.”

These on-the-ground consequences reflect the magnitude of the changes in the Pacific Ocean, where El Niños develop when unusually warm waters build up. These episodes occur every two to seven years and have contributed to planetary swings going back millenniums. But this year’s is on track to be the strongest in nearly 80 years of records.

Scientists are debating whether human-caused climate change is tilting the odds toward stronger and more frequent El Niño events. The El Niños of the past few decades have been comparably strong. But the variables that combine to create an El Niño are complex, and some experts argue the recent trend could just be a random signal.

What’s clear is that El Niño’s gyrations are adding to the stronger storms, drier dry spells and fiercer wildfires that global warming is already bringing about. El Niño will magnify those phenomena in some regions and could lift global temperatures to record levels next year, as the heat from the Pacific spreads around the world.

“What we’ll see in 2027 is a sneak peak of what the new normal will be in 2035,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth, a nonprofit research organization. “We’ll see things that have never happened before in our history in terms of temperature, drought conditions, extreme heat.”

El Niño events are measured by looking at sea surface temperatures in a specific rectangular zone of the Pacific Ocean. Temperatures there have soared over the past three months, and forecasts suggest that, by year’s end, they could exceed normal levels by more than they did during the strongest El Niños in modern history, which occurred in 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16.

Between October and December, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says there’s an 81 percent chance that El Niño conditions will be “very strong,” meaning the three-month average temperature in that zone of the Pacific is 2 degrees Celsius, or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, higher than normal. But forecasts show that daily ocean temperatures during that period could spike to more than 3 degrees Celsius above normal.

“Maybe it doesn’t sound that big: three or even four degrees. We see that temperature variation over the course of a day,” said Samantha Stevenson-Karl, an associate professor and climate modeler at the University of California, Santa Barbara. “But the ocean doesn’t change that much. Like, ever.”

The extra heat in the waters of the Pacific affects air temperatures, too. For the first months of the year, 2026 was clearly cooler than 2024, the planet’s hottest year on record. But Dr. Hausfather still gives 2026 a 40 percent chance of being Earth’s warmest year on the books, a sign of how the pendulum could be swinging. According to NOAA, last month tied July 2024 as the world’s warmest July since global record-keeping began in 1850.

El Niño causes big shifts in the winds that blow moist air across the oceans, and the effects on rain-fed agriculture are already emerging in some regions. By the end of the year, El Niño could cause nearly 50 million more people across the globe to experience acute hunger, an increase of roughly a fifth, according to the United Nations World Food Program.

At the western end of the tropical Pacific, El Niño has led to a dry summer in parts of Southeast Asia, delaying the sowing of rice and other crops in Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and the Philippines. In India, monsoon rains have picked up in some regions in recent weeks, though large areas of the country remain in a rainfall deficit.

At the other end of the Pacific, El Niño has delayed planting and disrupted crop growth in Central America. Rainfall in Guatemala was as much as 85 percent below average in July, and the stress on crops has been compounded by well-above-normal temperatures.

In Panama, the dry stretch has raised concerns about operations in the Panama Canal. During the last El Niño, in 2023-24, a severe rain deficit snarled traffic in the waterway, which raises and lowers ships through the locks using water from a rain-fed lake.

As El Niño has gained strength, the Panama Canal Authority has tightened limits on how heavily loaded ships can be while crossing. Officials haven’t ruled out restricting daily transits, according to a statement last week from a spokesman for the canal authority, Octavio Colindres.

It’s hard to predict just how much below normal Central America’s rainfall will be in the coming months, said Steven Paton, who monitors the oceans and atmosphere at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama.

The reason, he said, is that scientists’ computer models are trained on past events. This year’s El Niño is expected to be so much stronger than any episode on record that we can’t be sure how accurately the models will anticipate its effects.

“At the very least, it’s going to be as bad as the worst we’ve seen before, possibly much worse,” Mr. Paton said.

In East Africa, El Niño usually brings heavy rain, and even floods and landslides, from November through January. But when the phenomenon appears earlier in the year, it can suppress rainfall in parts of the region, including western Kenya and Ethiopia.

That’s been the dire reality in recent months, said Chris Shitote, a field scientist based in Nairobi, Kenya, for the Famine Early Warning Systems Network, an agency under the U.S. State Department.

Mr. Shitote and some colleagues recently traveled through Kenya’s western grain-producing counties. The maize harvest was stunningly bad, he said. “It’s something some of us have not seen for the maybe 10 years we’ve been going out.”

Plants that normally grow to be nine feet tall topped out at just five or six feet, Mr. Shitote said. A typical harvest might yield 20 to 30 bags of corn for each acre of field, growers told him. This year, it looks like it could be just one or two bags per acre.

item.title: More Than 40 Dead After a Ferry Capsizes on Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba
item.description:
At least 44 people are dead and an unknown number are still missing a day after a crowded ferry overturned in Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba, the country’s president said on Wednesday.

“It is with a heavy heart and profound sadness that I learned of the tragic capsizing,” said Emmerson Mnangagwa, president of Zimbabwe, in a statement on Wednesday about the accident, which occurred on Tuesday and has raised questions about the ferry’s safety and operations.

He thanked private citizens and government security teams, noting that “without their swift response, many more lives would have been lost in the rough and choppy conditions” on the lake that day.

While dozens of people have been rescued — at least 67, the Zimbabwe police said — the search for more missing continued through Wednesday and will resume on Thursday.

Still, just how many passengers may have been on board the ferry when it capsized is unclear, the authorities say. There are indications that the vessel was packed well beyond its designated capacity, the police noted.

The ferry was run by the Rural Infrastructure Development Agency, a quasi-governmental department tasked with the development and maintenance of infrastructure, water supplies, roads services and more. The boat had an official capacity of 90 passengers, excluding crew, but initial indications suggested there were about 120 passengers on the vessel when it overturned, according to the national police.

Based on their investigations, the police suspect the true number could have been even higher, officials said.

The vessel left from the resort town of Kariba and was headed to Chalala, a remote fishing camp on the shores of Lake Kariba, which is the world’s largest man-made lake by volume. According to a declaration of disaster by the president, it capsized after being struck by strong waves while navigating near Long Island, an island about 10 miles from Kariba.

The Department of Civil Protection is coordinating a search and rescue response with the national police’s underwater unit, the Zimbabwe National Army Boat Squadron, local authorities and others. A privately owned helicopter from the Matusadonha Conservation Trust, a national park, has also been deployed to support aerial search efforts, according to the presidential declaration.

Zimbabwe’s public broadcaster said on Wednesday evening that search and rescue operations had stopped for the night and would resume again on Thursday, with divers concerned that there were still people trapped inside the capsized ferry. It said that there are plans to tow the ferry to a nearby island.

“This tragedy has exposed serious deficiencies in our maritime capabilities which we have to address immediately so that our places of recreation do not become death traps to the innocent,” Mr. Mnangagwa said, in an apparent reference to the ferry being overcrowded. And he directed all agencies associated with maritime safety, including specialized units within the security forces, “to take an active interest in ensuring remedial interventions” in light of Tuesday’s accident.

Mr. Mnangagwa called on Zimbabweans to “unite in prayer for the souls of the departed, for the success of the ongoing search operations, speedy recovery of survivors and for comfort and strength for the bereaved families.”

item.title: Scenes From the 2026 European Solar Eclipse
item.description:
Flocks of sky-watchers around Europe turned their gazes upward on Wednesday for the rare chance to witness a total solar eclipse, the continent’s first in decades.

The eclipse began just after 6 p.m. Central European Time (around 12 p.m. Eastern time) in the northernmost part of Russia. The shadow of the moon swooped down to Greenland and Iceland, then farther south across parts of Spain. By 9 p.m., the eclipse ended as the sun set in the Mediterranean.

From the far-flung edges of Iceland to coastal Spain, locals and millions of visitors settled in for the event. The possibility of a couple of moments cloaked in darkness during daytime felt welcome during a summer when Europe has been baked by endless solar heat. But cloudy conditions, wildfire smoke and storm systems put a damper on the celestial show in some locations.

Fans watched the eclipse through protective glasses inside a stadium in Salzburg, Austria, before a soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa.

item.title: Afghanistan’s Unhappy Anniversary
item.description:
Afghanistan has a track record of defeating superpowers. The mujahedeen humbled the Soviet Union in the 1980s, and five years ago the Taliban pushed out the United States.

But can Afghanistan’s rulers overcome the discontent of their own people?

With the country on the verge of another all-out war, this time with Pakistan, that is less than certain. Today, my colleague Elian Peltier explains why all the ingredients for things to spiral out of control are there.

By Elian Peltier

The Taliban took over Afghanistan five years ago this week. They pushed out the world’s most powerful army. Yet the mood among Taliban officials I’ve spoken with and soldiers I’ve bumped into at checkpoints hasn’t exactly been celebratory — more like embattled.

On what could have been a triumphant anniversary for the group, the Taliban find themselves in crisis at home and abroad.

They face a conflict just short of open war with neighboring Pakistan. They’re dealing with fresh waves of attacks from armed groups who want to topple them. Add to that mass unemployment, near-total international isolation and growing domestic discontent, and it all amounts to the most serious threats the Taliban have encountered since their victory in 2021.

It’s too early to tell whether all this will escalate in a way that could threaten the regime’s survival. But it has cracked the thin veneer of security and stability that the Taliban herald as their primary achievement since taking over — and their primary selling point to the world.

A tight grip on power — and yet

The Taliban are holding Afghan society in a chokehold that spares no one. Girls and women face restrictions to a degree unseen anywhere else in the world. Religious minorities are witnessing the forced closure of their places of worship. Anyone who voices criticism is repressed.

That grip on power over a country of nearly 45 million people seems immovable. The Taliban collect taxes and are pretty good at it. They are building roads, dams and canals. European countries are desperate to work with them to deport Afghan migrants and asylum seekers. And when someone shuts the door on them, as Pakistan did when it closed its border last year, they open new ones: Afghanistan has increasingly relied on trade with Iran, India and Central Asian states like Uzbekistan.

And yet the signs of trouble that have appeared in recent months are impossible to ignore.

An underequipped Afghan Army waits nervously at the border with Pakistan. Once a sponsor of the Taliban, Pakistan has launched dozens of airstrikes on Afghanistan in recent months; killed 500 civilians since October, according to the United Nations; and threatened to go all in against the Taliban regime, which it accuses of harboring militants who are staging attacks on Pakistani territory.

The mistrust goes both ways: The Taliban have accused Pakistan of supporting the armed groups that have attacked Taliban outposts in Afghanistan’s northeastern province of Badakhshan and are gearing up for a sustained offensive.

Whether, or to what extent, Pakistan is actively supporting anti-Taliban groups is not clear, but suspicions are high enough that a senior Western diplomat with decades of experience working on Afghanistan told me this summer, “This region doesn’t need another proxy war.”

The picture on the domestic front is also grim. The Taliban are struggling to deal with a cascade of humanitarian and economic crises. Nearly four million Afghans have been forcibly returned from Iran and Pakistan since January 2025 — one of the world’s largest episodes of reverse migration in decades. Aid cuts have plunged millions into deeper food insecurity. And UNESCO says the Taliban have deprived 2.4 million Afghan girls of a secondary education — the equivalent of all school-age girls in New York, Mexico City and Moscow combined, forced to stay home indefinitely.

A society can withstand only so much, even under the tightest of grips. At a rare protest in June, demonstrators chanted “Work, education, freedom,” similar to what their Iranian neighbors chanted in 2022. And the leader of a large religious minority warned the Taliban in May: Don’t squeeze Afghan society too much, or it will explode.

The potential to spiral?

The Taliban know the world wants a stable Afghanistan — one that isn’t a source of refugees, opium or terrorism.

The Taliban claim the country no longer poses a security threat to the region or the West. They say that they have cracked down on the Islamic State, and that they want peaceful relations based on trade and diplomacy, including with the U.S.

All of this may have some truth to it. The Taliban don’t want their various crises to spiral. But it also might not be entirely up to them.

All the ingredients for things to get out of control in Afghanistan again are here, analysts say: Growing animosity toward Pakistan and a vast population of unemployed young Afghans are fertile ground for radicalization, especially as economic opportunities are nearly nonexistent. Under the Taliban, Afghanistan is, once again, a pariah state, with barely any allies.

As a foreign military official in Afghanistan put it, the country is no longer the hub for jihadism that it used to be — but it has everything it needs to become one again.

The past five years have brought some predictability and an end to almost two decades of fighting, which many Afghans have welcomed, despite the immense hardship and repression. But Afghanistan remains shattered, and what always looked like a fragile peace is already at risk.

item.title: Settler Siege of Palestinian Homes Highlights Growing West Bank Chaos
item.description:
Two Palestinian families have been trapped since Sunday inside their homes on a rocky West Bank hillside by a group of violent Israeli settlers, who set up a tent in the front yard of one of the houses. Residents say about 10 to 15 settlers have been attacking them around the clock, throwing stones and an ax.

Early Wednesday morning, after news of the siege began to draw news attention, the Israeli army’s commander for the West Bank, Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth, showed up in the village of Qusra and listened as one of the families described how the settlers had been terrorizing them since January. Outside, his soldiers tried to disperse the settlers with tear gas.

Yet, by 10:20 a.m., videos from security cameras show, the soldiers had left. Soon after, residents said, the settlers resumed their attacks.

“We had some hope in the morning when we saw that the army was present,” Aisha Hassan, 35, who was in the meeting with General Bluth, said by telephone, even as she said one of the settlers was throwing stones at her. “But when we saw that the army could not stop the settlers — now, honestly, we are more afraid.”

On Wednesday evening, the army said in response that it was assigning an extra battalion to the West Bank to try to “strengthen order and operational control in the area.”

The army’s initial retreat and broader struggle to contend with settler violence cast a spotlight on the increasingly chaotic situation in the West Bank, where hundreds of Israeli settlers have been terrorizing Palestinians with near-impunity all year.

As of late July, 18 Palestinians have been killed by settlers, one more than in all of 2025, according to U.N. data. Settlers have been boasting on social media of their attacks, posting videos showing mosques that have been torched in Palestinian towns.

At times, soldiers have taken part in the violence, Palestinian and Israeli officials say, reflecting disciplinary problems that the military has acknowledged are an issue.

“It’s a great fiasco,” said Gadi Shamni, a retired two-star general and former head of Israel’s Central Command, whose area of responsibility included the occupied territory. “There’s a loss of control over the West Bank.”

Israel’s right-wing, pro-settler government says that concerns about settler violence are overblown, and officials have repeatedly signaled their support for Israelis accused of attacks. The defense minister, Israel Katz, boasts of having stripped the army of the authority to issue detention orders for settlers — which had been a key tool for restraining Israeli extremist violence. In July, he visited in prison a settler arrested as a key suspect in the sexual assault of a Palestinian man in March and clashed with General Bluth over the suspect’s detention.

In Qusra, located near the city of Nablus in the northern West Bank, the violence has afflicted two families in particular: the Hassans and their neighbors the Abu Ridis.

Louai Abu Ridi, 46, a native of Qusra who immigrated to Ohio in 2003 and is a U.S. citizen in the gas-station business, said he had poured about $1 million into building a house in his birthplace. The settler attacks, beginning in January, started to lay waste to his investment, he said. His brother moved into the house to try to protect it.

Mr. Abu Ridi said he had appealed to the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem for help and was told to report the attacks to the Israeli authorities. An embassy spokesman did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

Ms. Hassan, whose brothers Yusuf and Rizq built two other homes on land owned by their father, said that settlers had broken windows and doors, cut utility lines, destroyed solar panels and stolen the birthday gifts a 2-year-old had received days earlier.

Residents said the settlers appeared to be based in an unfinished home outside Qusra. In March, witnesses said, settlers based in that same home killed another Qusra man, Amir Odeh, and beat and stabbed his father.

Sometimes the settlers have tried to intimidate the families, grazing sheep on their land and destroying their plantings. But the violence has escalated, Ms. Hassan said. Settlers once tried to push the family’s cooking-gas tank into the house through an open window, she said. They’ve fired gunshots and thrown Molotov cocktails at the house, she added.

Efforts by New York Times reporters on Wednesday to reach the scene and speak with the settlers and residents were rendered fruitless by roadblocks guarded by soldiers and settlers.

On Sunday, after the settlers set up camp just outside the Hassans’ homes and erected a tent, the family called the police. When an Israeli soldier showed up, Ms. Hassan said, he ignored the family and instead greeted the settlers warmly. Video recordings show him joining the settlers in prayers.

On Monday night, when Ms. Hassan’s 2-year-old niece, Hoor, spiked a fever and the family called an ambulance, she said, settlers blocked the ambulance and, the driver said, tried to ram it with an all-terrain vehicle. Late Tuesday afternoon, other soldiers made it possible for another ambulance to take the girl to a local clinic, Ms. Hassan recounted.

The military issued a statement on Tuesday acknowledging reports of Israelis seizing Palestinian homes and land in Qusra and expressing “condemnation” for what it called “illegal, reprehensible and unacceptable” actions. On Wednesday, it said that disciplinary action would be taken against the “security personnel involved.”

General Shamni, the retired Central Command chief, said that what had allowed him to keep the Israeli-occupied West Bank relatively calm during his tenure, from 2007 to 2009 — close cooperation with the Israeli police, the Internal Security Agency and the military’s Civil Administration — could no longer be counted on. Pro-settler extremists, like the cabinet ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, wield too much influence over all those agencies, General Shamni said.

Moreover, he added, the military units serving in the West Bank are largely composed of soldiers who grew up in the settlements. “They are the settlers,” he said. “That’s the problem.”

General Shamni said he wished that President Trump would force Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has minimized settler violence, to crack down on it.

General Bluth’s visit to Qusra on Wednesday appeared to signal a new resolve to address the situation, but it evidently alarmed the settlers. The young men who had been attacking the Qusra homes were quickly joined by scores more, who could be seen throwing stones onto the road to make it impassable and then scuffling with soldiers, according to witnesses and video viewed by a reporter.

Soldiers confiscated a tarp and an all-terrain vehicle but ultimately drove off, leaving the settlers behind.

They were still there on Wednesday night.

Gabby Sobelman contributed reporting.

item.title: A City Mobilizes Against a Stubborn Health Threat: Mosquitoes
item.description:
It’s been 10 years, but Paulo Gomes still vividly remembers the terror he felt that his wife, Lucirene, would never return from the hospital, that she would die instead of the dengue she contracted from a mosquito bite, her body racked with fever and excruciating pain.

She did come home, after 15 days, and recovered fully after several more months. But the experience forever changed how Mr. Gomes thought about mosquitoes.

Mr. Gomes, now 65, is an eager participant in an aggressive campaign by Belém, the northern Brazilian city where he lives on the edge of a rain forest, to reduce mosquitoes and the health dangers they bring.

Municipal workers have counseled him that mosquitoes breed in standing water and thrive in musty, moist spaces. He fills the swimming pool in the backyard every Friday for his grandchildren who live nearby, but drains it religiously every Sunday after they leave.

He and his wife keep their veranda scrupulously clean and uncluttered, just a tricycle in one corner, a hammock in another — and, since last summer, a plastic bucket that is a centerpiece in Belém’s multipronged strategy against mosquitoes.

The size of a small trash can, it offers just the sort of dark, watery cavity a female mosquito might seek to lay eggs. But it contains larvicide, a chemical that kills young mosquitoes, and when she lands inside she becomes coated with it. When she flies away, she will spread it to other breeding sites, typically within a quarter-mile radius. Last year, Belém distributed 5,000 units in the parts of the city hit hardest by dengue.

At the moment, mosquitoes are a bigger menace in Belém and the rest of Brazil than in the United States or Europe, but the warming planet is expanding their range. Most cases of dengue, malaria and chikungunya in those places were contracted during travel abroad, but locally acquired cases are occurring more frequently. In 2024, the United States recorded nearly 3,800 cases of dengue, more than 100 of them locally acquired. About a third of the patients were hospitalized, and six died.

“The climate crisis is a public health crisis,” Dr. Alexandre Padilha, Brazil’s health minister, said in an interview.

“It’s not a coincidence” that during its Group of 20 presidency, Brazil championed new initiatives to combat climate-driven diseases like dengue, Dr. Padilha said. “We have a lot to learn and also to teach many regions in the U.S.A. about how to face the impact of climate change,” he said.

Forged by bitter experience, Brazil has embraced new techniques to combat mosquitoes. Most of them are environmentally friendly, including building the world’s largest “mosquito factory,” a facility that produces mosquitoes containing Wolbachia, a bacterium that blocks dengue and other viruses. The Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes are then released in communities to breed and pass the bacteria to the next generation.

Tackling mosquitoes requires more than gee-whiz science. Municipal departments will need to beef up their vector control divisions and budgets, doctors must be trained to recognize and treat the diseases, and the general public will need education on protecting itself.

“It’s important for other countries to get ready for the possibility of having more and more cases happening, and train all the layers of the society,” said Luciano Moreira, the chief executive of Wolbito do Brasil, a joint venture between the nonprofit World Mosquito Program and the Brazilian government.

“It’s not just something like the government just goes there and sprays,” he said. “It’s part of a movement.”

Locals like to say Belém has only two seasons — one in which it rains every day, and one when it rains all day.

The city is a gateway to the mighty Amazon, and it is edged by lush, muddy rainforest. Mango trees and their fallen fruit line the streets, luring insects with their sweet sticky scent. Small puddles of water — on the sidewalks, in stacked tires and in trash cans — offer mosquitoes the perfect nurseries to grow millions more of themselves.

For decades, Belém residents have been under attack by Aedes aegypti, the type of mosquito that carries dengue, Zika and chikungunya — so much so that in 2018, a city park installed a large fiberglass statue of the insect. (Aedes aegypti is also found in many parts of the United States, including Florida, Texas and California.)

Climate change has allowed these mosquitoes to multiply faster, intensifying the threats they carry. In 2024, dengue infected more than 10 million people in Brazil and killed more than 6,000. There might have been even more deaths if doctors in Brazil did not know how to recognize and treat the disease promptly, said Moises Silva, a microbiologist at the ⁠Federal University of Pará in Belém.

Brazil’s toll that year was about four times the previous number, and in Belém, it was about seven times higher, flooding the city’s hospitals and forcing a reckoning. City officials adopted myriad methods in response, from increasing common-sense solutions like garbage disposal and treatment of sewage to collaborating with academic scientists like Dr. Silva.

It was Dr. Silva who petitioned the health minister to include Belém in the list of 10 cities that would try out the special larvicide dispensing buckets, and to fund training and equipment for city workers.

Dr. Silva and his colleagues looked at the distribution of dengue cases across the city. They also factored in data from the city’s entomology lab on mosquito larvae and egg traps to gauge the size of the population that season.

Based on those two streams of information, they identified the most vulnerable areas, down to the street level, many of them in low-income neighborhoods and favelas, that would benefit from the units.

Unlike mosquito traps that kill females, the larvicide units, which cost less than $2 each, use the females to spread the chemical to breeding spots that would be hard for humans to find, Dr. Silva said. “We’re using the mosquito against the mosquito,” he said. “That’s the smart thing about the trap.”

The city also trained the workers to educate residents in the low-income areas on ways to keep mosquitoes at bay, to recognize dengue symptoms and to head to the hospital at the signs of severe illness. High fever, headache and vomiting can be mistaken for signs of many other diseases. But dengue also produces intense muscle and joint pain, which earned the disease the moniker “breakbone fever,” and may progress to leaky blood vessels and death if left untreated.

“Back in the day, there was a lot of focus in the wealthier area, so the center of the town, and so we spread that out,” Igor Normando, Belém’s mayor, said in an interview.

Because of these efforts, he said, mosquito-borne diseases in the city dropped by 70 percent last season.

“The success of this program was a result of the fact that we didn’t just focus on one specific thing,” Mr. Normando said. “We didn’t only focus on education and only rubbish collection and only this or that.”

A core part of Belém’s strategy is its community outreach. Of the city’s more than 1,000 workers in the health department, about a third are focused on limiting mosquito populations. (By contrast, Bay County, Fla., a coastal area of comparable size, has 15 full-time employees in its mosquito control division.)

Many of Belém’s so-called vector control agents go door to door, reminding residents about ways to keep their premises insect-free, keeping water containers covered and mopping up wet spots after the day’s inevitable rainfall. The houses that have the larvicide dissemination units get a monthly visit to replenish supplies and to ensure that the containers have not been refashioned to pot plants or to launder clothes.

On a sweltering day last month, workers on door-to-door rounds discovered that one homeowner’s grandson had thrown the container away when cleaning, not realizing its purpose. Another family hid the container behind two bicycles, to prevent their dogs from getting to it.

As a shirtless Mr. Gomes tried to stay cool in the unrelenting heat, Elizabete Reis, the city agent, inspected the bucket in his veranda for mosquito larvae — there were none — then dumped the water and refilled it. She then added a fresh mesh strip coated with the larvicide, which sticks to female mosquitoes as they land on the strip to lay eggs.

Mr. Gomes said he was “fascinated” to hear that Belém was ahead of many American cities in adopting this approach. “We imagine that this would be something that you would already have, and we always expect these solutions to be coming from the U.S., not for us to be exporting them,” he said.

Most cities in the United States still rely on aerial or truck spraying to control mosquitoes, dispatching the trucks after dusk and warning citizens to stay indoors. The pesticides can cause dizziness, nausea and skin irritation in some people, trigger seizures in some pets and wipe out beneficial insects like bees and butterflies. Brazil, too, initially relied heavily on spraying, but by the early 2000s, the mosquitoes had begun to show signs of resistance to the chemicals. Cities like Belém now resort to fogging — which produces a fine mist rather than the big droplets from sprays — only during outbreaks.

“We cannot just ban the use of insecticides, but we need to use them in a more rational way,” said Dr. Moreira of Wolbito do Brasil. Ideally, insecticides would become part of a larger strategy, to be used mainly during outbreaks, he said, “so that’s what Brazil is doing.”

In 2016, amid widespread insecticide resistance, Brazil’s health ministry convened experts to brainstorm new solutions, including breeding mosquitoes containing Wolbachia bacteria. Wolbachia is an environmentally harmless solution, naturally present in about half of all insects. The technological marvel here was in introducing the bacteria into Aedes aegypti.

The approach is now part of the country’s mosquito-control strategy in 16 cities, but the government plans to expand that number to nearly 80 by the end of next year, Dr. Moreira said.

Belém is not yet on the list to release Wolbachia mosquitoes; it may do so after reducing the numbers with other methods first. But for some residents, the city’s strategy of distributing larvicide units has already brought back unexpected magic.

Filipe Borges, 63, recalled that when Belém sent trucks to fumigate his neighborhood decades ago, the electric blue Amazonian butterflies of his childhood disappeared. But now, he said, there are noticeably fewer mosquitoes in his yard, and yet “the butterflies are back.”

item.title: What to Know About Today’s U.K. Special Election: Farage vs. Binface
item.description:
Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform U.K., Britain’s populist right-wing party, will face voters on Thursday in a special election that he initiated, hoping to return to Parliament weeks after resigning amid investigations into possible financial impropriety.

Mr. Farage, who is under investigation for failing to declare a 5 million pound gift (about $6.7 million) from a British crypto-billionaire in Thailand, has said he hopes that a new mandate from his constituents in Clacton, a coastal area in Essex, England, will show that his voters do not care about the issue.

He said that he has been the subject of “constant demonization” by the press and his critics. The investigations into his finances, he claims, are proof that the “establishment have now decided that they can’t beat us fairly, so they’ve chosen to use foul means.”

After he resigned to force the new special election, all of Britain’s major parties boycotted it, calling it a stunt. Mr. Farage’s most significant opponent is a novelty candidate named Count Binface, who campaigns wearing a trash can over his head.

Here’s what to know about Thursday’s vote.

As the leader of Reform U.K., Mr. Farage is the most prominent right-wing populist in Britain, focused on campaigning against immigration and in favor of lower taxes and fewer regulations, particularly on cryptocurrency.

A veteran politician who campaigned for more than two decades for Britain to leave the European Union, and who has led several parties, Mr. Farage is an ally of President Trump and has styled himself in a similar way. He has long warned of an “invasion” of migrants and railed against the establishment in Westminster.

For most of the last year, Reform led national opinion polls amid widespread concern about rising prices, taxes, migration and dissatisfaction with Keir Starmer, the former Labour prime minister.

In May, Mr. Farage led Reform to its biggest electoral success ever. The party won almost 1,500 seats on municipal councils. But overall, Reform won only about 26 percent of the vote, down from more than 30 percent the previous year.

And the party has lost several parliamentary by-elections that it had hoped to win in recent months, including in Gorton and Denton, which was won by the Green Party, and in Makerfield, where Labour’s Andy Burnham easily beat the Reform candidate.

The polls have shown a continued decline for Reform in recent weeks, as the accusations about improper disclosure of financial support have increased. Several recent polls have shown support for the party falling under 25 percent and Labour taking the lead.

Earlier this year, Britain’s parliamentary standards commissioner, Daniel Greenberg, confirmed that he was investigating whether Mr. Farage had broken parliamentary rules by not disclosing the £5 million gift from Christopher Harborne, the crypto billionaire.

Mr. Farage has said he did not need to disclose the gift, but has offered a variety of conflicting explanations for why Mr. Harborne gave him the money in the weeks before he won his seat in Parliament in 2024.

He initially said it was for his personal security amid threats. In his resignation speech, he said that he gets “daily online calls for me to be murdered” and has run up “very, very substantial bills to make sure that I was safe.”

But in an interview in May, Mr. Farage said the money was “a reward for campaigning for Brexit.”

Critics of Mr. Farage have pointed out that since he entered Parliament, he has championed the cryptocurrency industry and that Reform has pushed for light-touch regulation.

In his resignation speech, Mr. Farage referred to the standards investigation into the Harborne gift, but also said that “yet another standards investigation is underway.” That comment came days after The Sunday Times of London reported that one of his close aides, George Cottrell, had provided undisclosed benefits to Mr. Farage including security, social media employees and accommodation.

Mr. Farage did not intend to stay out of office for long.

In his remarks last month announcing his resignation, he said that “the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions. This will be a people-versus-the-establishment by-election. It’s a chance to stick two fingers up to the entire establishment, to frankly tell them where to go.”

Reform officials were always very confident that Mr. Farage would recapture his seat in Parliament. The last time he ran in Clacton, during the 2024 general election, he won with 46.2 percent of the vote. The Conservative Party candidate came second with 27.9 percent.

But Mr. Farage and his advisers hoped to use the election to change the political narrative and give him a prominent victory over his major rival political parties. Instead, all of the main parties said they would not put forward candidates, preferring to wait for the results of the parliamentary investigation.

That makes it more likely that Mr. Farage will win a landslide, while making it harder for him to argue that he defeated “the establishment.”

Count Binface is a character played by Jon Harvey, 46, a writer and comedian who is part of Britain’s long tradition of novelty political candidates. He describes himself as an intergalactic space warrior from the planet Sigma IX. His campaign pledges include a promise to build “at least one affordable house” and to “cut your taxes and raise everyone else’s.”

Mr. Harvey — or, as he’s better known, Mr. Binface — has run in several recent elections. In the recent special election where Prime Minister Andy Burnham won with 24,927 votes, Mr. Binface received just 95. (Though that was more than twice the number of votes that Howling Laud Hope received as the candidate for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party.)

In a recent interview in The New York Times, Mr. Binface said, “If humans choose to vote for Nigel, that is democracy.” But with the major parties absent, “I seem to be his majesty’s opposition.”

He is not expected to win on Thursday.

Assuming that Mr. Farage wins, as expected, he will once again be a member of Parliament. But the investigations into his finances — and those of Reform U.K. — are unlikely to be resolved any time soon.

The parliamentary standards investigation could continue for weeks or months.

If the standards investigation concludes that Mr. Farage violated Parliament’s rules, he could be suspended, possibly prompting another special election. The Conservative Party has already said it would run a candidate in Clacton if that happens.

There is also a police investigation underway into the legality of two donations to Reform of £250,000 each from Mr. Cottrell’s mother, Fiona. In a statement last month, the Metropolitan Police said that two people had been questioned as part of the investigation, although no arrests have been made. Reform did not respond to requests for comment. Mr. Cottrell and Ms. Cottrell could not be reached for comment.

item.title: Former Catholic Bishop Is Convicted of Sexual Abuse, Australian News Outlets Say
item.description:
An Australian jury on Thursday found a former Catholic bishop guilty of sexually abusing two men, according to media reports.

The former bishop, Christopher Alan Saunders, 76, was found guilty of 13 sex offenses, including one count of sexual penetration without consent and 12 charges of indecent assault, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. He was acquitted of six other charges. Mr. Saunders, who was the bishop of the diocese of Broome, had pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

The current bishop of Broome, Tim Norton, released a statement after the verdict acknowledging “the courage of victims, survivors and other witnesses who came forward to express their truth.”

“We are deeply sorry for the hurt they have experienced. We are sorry for the shame they have endured,” Bishop Norton said.

The offenses date back to 2008, WA Today, an Australian online publication, said.

During the trial, the District Court of Western Australia heard that Mr. Saunders held gatherings where he gave alcohol and food to men, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. The network also said he touched young men with his feet and, in one case, engaged in oral sex without consent. The victims were young Indigenous men.

The Broome diocese spans the Kimberley region, an area larger than France in the far north of the state of Western Australia. It has a population of about 50,000, according to the diocese’s website.

Mr. Saunders, who was arrested in 2024, is scheduled to be sentenced on Sept. 21.

The verdict makes Mr. Saunders one of the most senior Catholic clerics in Australia to have been convicted of sexual abuse committed while serving in his post, WA Today said.

A higher-ranking Catholic cleric, Cardinal George Pell, who died in 2023, was convicted in 2018 of child sexual abuse, but Australia’s highest court later overturned the conviction.

A national inquiry into child sex abuse in 2017 found that more than 4,000 people had been abused as children in religious institutions, of whom 61.8 percent said the abuse had occurred in Catholic institutions.

Bishop Norton said in his statement on Thursday that he would visit parts of the Broome diocese in the coming months to speak with members of the community.

Mr. Saunders was consecrated as the second bishop of the diocese in 1996, but he stepped aside in 2020, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. He formally resigned from the position in 2021.

item.title: Hundreds of Flights Canceled in Sicily as Mount Etna Spews Volcanic Ash
item.description:
One of Sicily’s busiest airports has canceled more than 700 flights in the past week because of steady eruptions from Mount Etna, a volcano that has spewed millions of cubic yards of ash through eastern Sicily and its airspace.

Etna is one of Europe’s most active volcanoes, and its eruptions are frequent, said Salvatore Gambino, the director of a National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology observatory, which is situated on the mountain. But he said the current spell, which began on Aug. 6, was unusual because of the “sustained and continuous emission of ash.”

Steady southeast winds have been blowing plumes of ash from one of the volcano’s central craters toward the international airport in Catania, a major port city at Etna’s base.

Since Friday, the airport has closed, reopened and re-closed its airspace, causing headaches for tens of thousands of travelers at the height of Italy’s summer vacation season, and just before Ferragosto, a national holiday that falls on Saturday.

Sicily’s regional government and the Catania airport authority have organized train and bus shuttle services for passengers whose flights are diverted to other Sicilian airports, including in Palermo and Trapani, on the island’s western coast.

Still, passengers have camped out at Catania’s airport and slept on luggage carousels, Italian news media reported. Sicily’s government said it had stationed volunteer teams at the airport to hand out water. Catania’s airport authority did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Catania’s tourism office said it could not estimate how many tourists were stranded. “We are sincerely sorry for what is happening these days and for all the potential inconveniences that the situation on Etna is causing,” Lucia Caffo, the office’s head of tourist promotion and development, wrote in an email.

A Sicilian business association estimated that the disruptions could cost $15 million to $29 million in lost tourism revenue.

Dr. Gambino said it was “absolutely impossible” to predict how much more ash Etna would spew, for how much longer and where the wind would send it. As of Thursday, the volcano’s activity was holding steady, he said.

“It could end tomorrow, in a few days, in a week, or in a month,” he said.

item.title: Who Are the Houthis?
item.description:
The Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen have waded into a widening war in the Middle East, announcing a blockade on ships linked to Saudi Arabia and carrying out strikes on cargo vessels.

Fears are growing that the Houthis, who control much of Yemen, may be on the verge of a new civil war with the country’s Saudi-backed government.

Violence had abated after a truce took hold in 2022. Since then, Yemen has been effectively divided into two states, with the Houthis in control of large swaths of the north. Recent hostilities threaten to reignite a conflict that, for over a decade, has created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

On Tuesday, Yemen’s government accused the Houthis of carrying out missile strikes on a cargo ship in the Red Sea, killing at least six people. The Yemeni Transport Ministry said in a statement that the vessel, Tihamah, had been carrying food supplies. The Houthi military confirmed that its forces had targeted a ship in the Bab al-Mandab Strait but said the vessel had been carrying “Saudi military equipment.”

Attacks on vessels transiting the Red Sea have coincided with a spike in violence in Yemen, with the Houthis carrying out missile and drone strikes on government-controlled cities. The Yemeni government has launched counterattacks, and the escalating violence has threatened to tip the country back into a full-scale war.

Here’s what to know about the Houthis and how this conflict affects the region and the world.

The Houthis, also called Ansar Allah, are Shiite Muslim militants who have been fighting Yemen’s internationally recognized government for about two decades, framing themselves as anticorruption, anti-Western nationalists. They overran the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in 2014, forcing the government to flee to the southern city of Aden.

The following year, a Saudi-led coalition launched a bombing campaign to oust the Houthis but failed, leaving the group in power in northern Yemen. Hundreds of thousands of people died, some from violence and many more from the resulting famine and disease. The United Nations estimated in 2025 that 4.5 million people in Yemen were displaced as a result of the conflict.

The Houthis oppose Israel and the United States. The militants are part of the so-called axis of resistance led by Iran, along with the armed groups Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

The Houthi ideology is reflected in the slogan its members shout at rallies: “God is great, death to America, death to Israel, a curse upon the Jews, victory to Islam.”

Once a ragtag group of poorly organized rebels, the Houthis bolstered their arsenal to include cruise and ballistic missiles, along with long-range drones. Analysts attributed this expansion to support from Iran.

Unlike other Iran-backed militant groups in the Middle East, the Houthis did not originate with direct support from Iran. They are neither a complete proxy for Iranian interests in Yemen nor fully independent of Tehran’s influence. The Houthis have always weighed loyalty to Tehran alongside their own domestic political calculations.

When the Houthis launched strikes on Israel in March, the group said it was intervening in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran to help its regional allies.

It was the first Houthi strike on Israel since the United States brokered a cease-fire between Israel and Hamas in October.

In the months after that attack, the Houthis remained on the sidelines. Some experts said the group had been weakened by a weekslong bombardment by the United States and Israel last year and was reluctant to expend too much of its dwindling arsenal.

But last month, hostilities erupted again. The Houthi authorities accused Saudi Arabia of attacking Yemen’s main international airport, in Sanaa, after an Iranian plane tried to land there. A rapid escalation followed, including strikes on ships, ports and cities, signifying a dangerous new phase for the region.

With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed by Iran for months, the Red Sea has become a vital alternative route for the transportation of Saudi oil and gas. Analysts say that Iran most likely urged the Houthis to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea, choosing a moment when such escalation would benefit both Tehran and the Houthis.

For Iran, the Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers heighten the pressure on President Trump by further disrupting global energy markets, analysts say. For the Houthis, the attacks are a way to pressure Saudi Arabia, giving the group leverage as it demands financial and political concessions from the kingdom.

item.title: Putin Visits Islands Seized from Japan in World War II, Angering Tokyo
item.description:
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia on Thursday visited islands seized from Japan at the end of World War II for the first time, prompting an angry rebuke from Tokyo.

Mr. Putin used the visit to reassert Russia’s territorial claims and to protest Japan’s ongoing sanctions against Russia over the invasion of Ukraine. A day before the visit, he said that Russia’s claim to the islands was a “reality” that had been “enshrined in international documents.”

“We are not threatening Japan. We have absolutely no claims against it,” Mr. Putin said. “On the contrary, Japan has territorial claims against our country.”

The visit, which came as Russia held large-scale military exercises in the neighboring seas, was the latest flare-up in tensions between the two countries. Russia has been putting pressure on Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, a defense hawk and critic of Moscow who was elected last year. She has pushed forward with Japan’s largest postwar defense buildup and sought closer ties with the United States.

Ms. Takaichi criticized the visit on Thursday, saying Japan had repeatedly warned Russian leaders to stay away from the islands, which are known in Russia as the southern Kuril Islands and in Japan as the Northern Territories. She described them as “an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law.”

She told reporters that Mr. Putin’s visit “hurts the feelings of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable.” Japan’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that it had summoned Russia’s ambassador to protest the visit.

Japan traces its claims to the 17th century, but the Russians generally date their sovereignty to the waning days of World War II, when Soviet troops occupied the islands after Japan’s surrender in 1945. Japan and Russia never signed a formal peace treaty after the war.

The islands stretch from the southern tip of the Kamchatka Peninsula in eastern Russia to Hokkaido in the northernmost part of Japan. Mr. Putin visited an island that is called Iturup in Russian and Etorofu in Japanese. He toured a fish-processing complex and ate caviar. He also visited a hospital and a school, the Kremlin said in a statement, releasing photos of the Russian leader’s stops.

The governor of the Sakhalin region, which includes the islands, Valery Limarenko, accompanied Mr. Putin on the visit. Under a bright sun, Mr. Putin met residents of the region and hugged two young children, in footage posted online by a state news reporter who follows the Russian leader.

“Look at this great weather, it’s like a resort!” Mr. Putin said. One woman responded that such weather is very rare, noting that it is usually windy and foggy. “The weather is smiling on you,” she said.

Mr. Putin’s visit is part of a broader tour across Siberia and the Far East that he has been making ahead of the Russian parliamentary election next month.

On Wednesday, during a visit to Russia’s Pacific Fleet in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, Mr. Putin boarded the Varyag guided missile cruiser. He said Japan had placed “unprovoked sanctions” on his country over the conflict in Ukraine and singled out Russia as an enemy threat.

The trip marks Mr. Putin’s first visit to the region claimed by Japan in his quarter century rule. President Dmitry A. Medvedev visited one of the islands in 2010, becoming the first Russian or Soviet leader to do so. Japan denounced the visit and summoned the Russian ambassador to Japan in protest.

Previous Japanese leaders, including former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, a mentor to Ms. Takaichi, made efforts to win back some of the territory.

But in 2019, hopes of a deal were dashed by Mr. Putin. He said that any agreement must have support from the public, which in Russia is strongly opposed to returning any islands to Japan.

Japan has made small efforts to improve relations with Russia in recent months, including sending a delegation of government officials to Moscow for trade talks and organizing cultural exchange trips. But it has maintained economic and trade sanctions against Moscow over the Ukraine war.

A recent investigation by The New York Times found that Russian military intelligence has been using Japan as a hub to source components for its war effort, exploiting weak Japanese espionage laws and high-tech industry.

Michito Tsuruoka, a professor at Keio University in Tokyo, said that Mr. Putin’s visit suggested that “there is no intention — particularly on the Russian side — to improve relations with Japan.”

“Russia’s narrative is that the deterioration of Japan-Russia relations is Japan’s fault,” he said. “From Japan’s perspective, of course, that is outrageous and untrue; the blame lies with Russia. It is essentially a case of ‘he said, she said,’ and Japan has no choice but to stand firm.”

Kiuko Notoya contributed reporting from Tokyo.

item.title: One Man’s Quest to Build India’s Most Livable City
item.description:
In one corner of the vast construction site, engineers are rerouting water into miles of canals that will spread like arteries around the new urban space.

In another, workers in hard hats are pouring concrete for a state-of-the-art building that will soon host India’s largest quantum computer — part of a broader project labeled “The Quantum Valley.”

Here, on what used to be banana groves and vegetable fields on the banks of the sacred River Krishna, the ambition of building India’s most livable city of the future is taking shape.

Erecting Amaravati as the new capital city for Andhra Pradesh, a state of 50 million people in India’s south, is an enormous task — the largest such exercise in urban planning in independent India. The country’s track record brings little confidence. Its major cities, marked by inadequate infrastructure and increasing pollution, have become notorious for failing to meet the needs of their massive populations.

The man who has taken it upon himself to change that is N. Chandrababu Naidu, the state’s 76-year-old chief minister. He has an obsessive eye for detail and a history of delivering projects of transformational scale. But he has also had setbacks, losing control of another state capital he helped build decades ago, along with legal battles and a stretch in the political wilderness.

Mr. Naidu has won the support of India’s powerful prime minister, Narendra Modi. He has set construction timelines in an effort to make the project an irreversible reality by the time his party faces re-election in 2029.

More than 25,000 people are working at the site on any given day, building a design by Norman Foster, the celebrated British architect. The city is laid out in grids and includes about a five-mile stretch of government buildings.

At the center of it all will be a high-spired legislative assembly building surrounded by a freshwater lake. Administrative offices will operate from five high-rise towers, which will accommodate 16,000 employees. The tallest, where the state’s chief minister will work, will have a helipad on its roof.

Sixty percent of the new city is expected to be covered by water or greenery, and it will include nearly 2,000 miles of cycling lanes.

Hundreds of millions of dollars have been committed for the 50-acre campus in the city’s “Quantum Valley.” Come January, the building will host a 156-qubit IBM quantum computer in the campus’s anchor building, which has seismic protection against even the smallest vibrations. Eight towers that will house 88,000 engineers are planned by the end of 2029.

Mr. Naidu lives by the construction site.

When he leaves his residence and turns left toward the makeshift government offices, he sees piles of sewer pipes waiting to go underground, mounds of dirt and scattered machinery. The young bougainvillea flowers in the road dividers are abloom, signaling hope that his city will rise.

The challenges are many: There was a drop of as much as 15 percent in the labor force because workers returned to their home states to cast votes in elections, while fuel prices rose as a result of the war in the Middle East. Mr. Naidu’s ambitions will also have to be tested against a routine reality in India — scandals around the failings of newly built infrastructure, from bridges collapsing to an airport flooding.

Vijay Rama Raju V, the official tasked by Mr. Naidu with overseeing the project, said the state is looking to showcase a new standard that modern India can deliver.

“It’s not that money is not there anymore. In India we cannot say that anymore,” he said.

For Mr. Naidu, Amaravati is at once about redemption and legacy.

In the late 1990s, he helped turn Hyderabad, then the capital of Andhra Pradesh, into a tech hub. He brought in giants like Microsoft and nurtured a local talent pool that has since produced leaders in some of the world’s largest tech companies.

But in 2014, the state of Andhra Pradesh was cleaved into two. Mr. Naidu became the chief minister of the newly truncated Andhra Pradesh and Hyderabad went to the newly created state of Telangana.

He has described the loss of Hyderabad as the worst day of his political career. Andhra Pradesh was not only deprived of a major source of revenue, but also an aspirational symbol of technological prowess. The part of the state Mr. Naidu was left in charge of was steeped in debt and lacked a proper city to house its seat of power.

Mr. Naidu was not available to be interviewed during our visit. His son Nara Lokesh, who leads several key ministries in his father’s government, described the period as demoralizing.

“You’re just thrown out one fine morning saying ‘get out, it’s not yours anymore,’” he said.

In 2014, the family left Hyderabad by helicopter and landed at the airport in Vijayawada, the region where work on a new capital would eventually begin.

“It was nothing but a tin shed. And I had tears,” Mr. Lokesh said about the airport. “It hurt, but that’s what gave us that fire, that energy to say ‘I will beat them.’ ”

The government began pooling 35,000 acres of land from 30,000 farmers for the new city, named Amaravati after a second-century capital of the ancient Andhra kingdom. Mr. Naidu was bent on the project despite an expert committee advising him against establishing a concentrated capital and urging him instead to decentralize government. Critics accused him of chasing a vanity project and wasting valuable fertile land. Like many leaders in South Asia, Mr. Naidu admires the city-state of Singapore for its efficiency and productivity. So he sought help from its government on a master plan.

When he faced resistance from some of the farmers, he introduced modest annuity payments until they received smaller but more valuable plots of developed land. He arranged for small groups of them to go to Singapore and visualize his vision of a shiny city that they could not see in their banana groves.

But, for a while, it all fell apart: Mr. Naidu was voted out of office in 2019.

He was accused of corruption and nepotism by his onetime ally, Mr. Modi. While in opposition, the state authorities sent him to jail for weeks in 2023, on charges that were dropped once he returned to power. In the five years that he was out of power, work on Amaravati stopped. His successor floated alternative ideas for a capital city.

Then, Mr. Naidu was returned to office in elections two years ago.

He made up with Mr. Modi, and attained the status of a kingmaker in the prime minister’s national coalition, giving him leverage. Mr. Modi helped him pass legislation declaring Amaravati as Andhra Pradesh’s undisputed capital city. And Mr. Naidu is using the good graces of New Delhi to bring in billions of dollars in loans to finance the building of the new city’s core.

His mantra is, “Speed, speed, speed.”

The nearby Quantum Valley is Mr. Naidu’s play for an economic engine and tech identity to propel his new city — much as software did in Hyderabad.

Late in 2024, months after taking office, he invited a group of scientists from South India’s premier technology institution, the IIT Madras, to his residence. The institute’s director, V. Kamakoti, appealed to Mr. Naidu’s ambitions by pitching what he saw as the technological race of the future: quantum computing.

Classical computing would not be able to meet the demands of the finance, agriculture and pharmaceutical industries, he told Mr. Naidu. While market benefits could be a couple of years away, Mr. Kamakoti said, the world’s major powers and largest tech companies were investing.

Mr. Naidu was sold.

“He is taking a leap of faith,” Mr. Kamakoti said.

Mr. Naidu wants his new capital city to be an ecosystem for quantum computing, including bringing in academic institutions to create a talent pipeline of quantum experts. He has drawn on lessons from Hyderabad that mastering software was not enough: India needs to start innovating hardware and to shape supply lines.

Last year, clicker in hand, Mr. Naidu gave a lecture that was broadcast to hundreds of thousands of university students across the state.

“Quantum offers India a rare chance to enter early, rather than catch up later,” he told the students. “You are all thinking tomorrow. I am thinking next 20 years.”

item.title: Whatever Happened to English Summers? Scorched Britons Would Like to Know.
item.description:
As Britons swelter under yet another heat wave, forecasters are warning that a brutal summer is on course to become the hottest yet.

The Met Office, Britain’s weather agency, issued an amber warning — the second highest level — for Thursday in large parts of southeast England.

The extreme heat has remade summer for a country where many once escaped abroad to feel the blazing sun on their skins.

“An English summer is not the same anymore,” said Jacqui Browne, 67, as she sat on the brown grass of a London park.

On Thursday, temperatures in London are expected to reach 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 degrees Fahrenheit), according to a forecast by the Met Office.

There was a time when British summers were more temperate and marked by rain, but drought conditions have left large parts of the country parched.

The north, for example, is not as cool or green as usual, said Ms. Browne’s sister Janice Kennedy, 66, who was visiting from there.

“Even up north it’s quite warm,” Ms. Kennedy said. “Not like down here, but it’s quite warm up there, as well.”

Some, like Ms. Browne and Ms. Kennedy, still remember the summer of 1976, when repeated long spells of hot and dry weather made it the benchmark for hot summers. Now, that seems almost quaint.

The summer of 2022 stands out in memory for its intensity. It was then that Britain recorded a temperature above 40 degrees Celsius for the first time, according to the Met Office.

“Now it’s been overshadowed by the last three or four years,” Ms. Browne said.

By the end of this past July, Britain had already recorded 37 days of extreme heat, nearing a record set in 1995, when 39 days were recorded, according to figures from the weather agency.

Even if the last weeks of August are slightly cooler, the weather is still likely to break existing records, according to Met Office predictions.

“Another record-breaking summer now looks increasingly likely for the U.K., following the second-warmest June and second-warmest July on record, and yet another heat wave imminent,” Mike Kendon, the Met Office’s senior scientist, said in a statement this week.

“These statistics are a clear reminder — if one were needed — of the stark changes that we are seeing in the U.K.’s climate,” Mr. Kendon said.

Determining how a single heat event was influenced by climate change requires specific attribution studies. But scientists are certain that heat waves around the world are generally becoming more intense, more frequent and longer.

The heat has persuaded some to rethink how they spend their summers.

“I think you might find that is a real win for coastal towns,” Mike Jones, 55, said as he and friends cooled off in a London park. “I think there’ll be more staycations, too.”

His friend Caroline John noted a downside.

“When you go abroad, you have a cocktail and the sea,” she said. “Whereas, in London, you’re on the tube in the heat.”

The sweltering subway system is just one example of a region not built for heat, both agreed. Train lines have buckled in the heat, causing many delays over the summer.

“We’re not equipped, are we?” Ms. John, 50, said.

Britain’s weather agency warned that Thursday’s temperatures could affect heat-sensitive infrastructure in homes and businesses. And delays on the road and rail were expected, with potential health and welfare concerns for those stuck on the road.

The high temperatures could also lead to health complications for some, especially older people and those with vulnerabilities.

But for Anesta Logan, 61, who was in the park with Mr. Jones and Ms. John, the new British summer is an improvement over the cool ones she grew up with, to say nothing of the freezing winters.

“The hotter, the better,” she said. “People are always going to complain.”

item.title: How China Remembers Zhu Rongji, the Premier Who Spoke His Mind
item.description:
Zhu Rongji, China’s former premier, is often remembered for opening the country to the global economy. But among Chinese people, his death has also prompted nostalgia for his blunt words and pugnacious outbursts, a contrast with the political rigidity of the present.

Xi Jinping, China’s autocratic leader, exercises tight control over political expression, and the public mourning of leaders is meticulously scripted. Major state-run news outlets carried the Communist Party’s official obituary of Mr. Zhu, who died aged 97 on Wednesday. Mr. Xi and other leaders are expected to attend a formal funeral and memorial service in the coming days, though no details have been announced.

The party’s obituary in the People’s Daily emphasized how Mr. Zhu pulled back some state controls of the economy and propelled China’s entry into global commerce from 1993 to 2003, first as vice premier and then as premier, the equivalent of a prime minister. It also said Mr. Zhu “dared to speak the truth and did not fear offending others.”

Some in China celebrated Mr. Zhu’s legacy and his frankness in bolder terms.

The deaths of senior leaders have become occasions for people to point indirectly to what they see as a more dynamic and hopeful past. On Chinese social media sites, many recalled with affection Mr. Zhu’s sometimes ebullient, sometimes combative style.

“They faced up to the opportunities of reform, they managed the pace of reform, they were the pillars of China’s economic reforms,” Rao Yi, the president of Capital Medical University in Beijing wrote in a tribute on Thursday to Mr. Zhu’s generation on WeChat, a popular Chinese social media platform. Dr. Rao did not mention Mr. Zhu by name.

Online commenters remembered Mr. Zhu’s gladiatorial news conferences and peppery phrases, a pointed reminder that these days, even senior Chinese officials often do little more than echo the words of Mr. Xi.

Some cited Mr. Zhu’s warning against corrupt officials, where he suggested the lengths he would go to attack the problem. “I’ve prepared 100 coffins,” Mr. Zhu said at a meeting in 1998. “99 of them are for corrupt officials, and I’m leaving one for myself.”

Others quoted Mr. Zhu’s description of poorly built flood barriers that broke under a deluge on the Yangtze River in 1998. “Tofu dregs construction, turtle eggs construction,” he said. (“Turtle eggs” has a more vulgar implication in Chinese than it does in English.)

The official memorializing of Mr. Zhu will likely follow the party’s scripted formula. The party’s obituary was roughly the same length and given similar prominence as the one for the former premier Li Keqiang in 2023, and for the another former premier, Li Peng, in 2019.

The deaths of former leaders can be politically sensitive in China. When Li Keqiang died unexpectedly in 2023 at age 68, there was widespread mourning online and in his hometown in Anhui Province. Experts saw the outpouring as an expression of public sympathy for an official who had been pushed aside by Mr. Xi.

A similar, highly visible mourning seems less likely for Mr. Zhu. He belonged to an older political generation, and had long receded from public life. Controls on expression in China have also tightened since 2023.

Some tributes to Mr. Zhu in China were tempered with recognition that he was not an unabashed economic liberalizer, nor did his promises always come to fruition, including his vows to clean out corruption and ease burdens on farmers.

“Zhu Rongji loudly declared that ‘the burden on farmers is too heavy,’ but whether through emotional appeals or rational arguments, the problem was never really solved,” said one essay that was shared on WeChat about Mr. Zhu’s legacy as premier.

Mr. Zhu focused on courting global business and not enough on the countryside, said Yasheng Huang, a professor at M.I.T. who has written extensively about China’s economic transformation.

He squeezed financial flows for rural factories that had mushroomed in the previous decade, forcing many of them to go out of business and taking the momentum out of rural development, Professor Huang said.

“We need to incorporate into our assessment what happened in rural China, which after all was 70 to 80 percent of the Chinese population,” Professor Huang wrote in emailed comments. “Zhu was a reformer but he was one in a way far more complex than often portrayed.”

Mr. Zhu is widely remembered abroad for negotiating China’s entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001. But in China he is also remembered for giving the central government in Beijing much greater control over revenues. That shift paved the way for the big-spending projects of later leaders, including Mr. Xi. Local governments, on the other hand, are often cash starved.

“Zhu Rongji was a leader who reflected the paradoxes of reform-era China: the pursuit of rapid economic growth paired with enduring political control,” said Julian Gewirtz, a China historian at Columbia University who is writing a book on U.S.-China relations after the Cold War. “Zhu himself bristled at Western efforts to fit him into familiar liberalizing archetypes.”

Ruoxin Zhang in Beijing and Amy Chang Chien in Taipei contributed research and reporting.
